reconcile.connective: Clarke and other harmonizers read James's peirasmos as trial in a positive sense, distinct from the enticement to sin the Lord's Prayer petitions against.

discrepancy.connective: NT scholar Andrew Bowden argues 'trial' is a mistranslation in James 1:2 — undercutting Clarke's own distinction from 'what is generally understood by...temptation.'

skeptic.name: Andrew Bowden
skeptic.work: "Count What All Joy? The Translation of πειρασμός in James 1.2 and 12," The Bible Translator 65.2
skeptic.attribution: Andrew Bowden, "Count What All Joy? The Translation of πειρασμός in James 1.2 and 12," The Bible Translator 65.2 (2014): 113–124.

excerpts.excerpt_text: The word πειρασμος, which we translate temptation, signifies affliction, persecution, or trial of any kind; and in this sense it is used here, not intending diabolic suggestion, or what is generally understood by the word temptation.
excerpts.on_tension_rationale: Clarke explicitly distinguishes James's peirasmos (trial/affliction) from 'what is generally understood by the word temptation' -- the same word used in Matthew 6:13 -- which is the exact lexical crux of the contradiction.

pd_work.resource: John Haley, An Examination of the Alleged Discrepancies of the Bible (1874), p. 253
pd_work.author: John Haley
pd_work.note: Haley's chapter of ethical discrepancies includes a dedicated 'Temptation. Desirable. / Undesirable.' entry citing exactly James 1:2 against Matthew 6:13, resolving it via Alford's distinction between the general sense of trial/distress and the narrower sense of enticement -- 'Matthew inculcates a humble self-distrust and shrinking from such trials in the prospect; James teaches that when they do providentially overtake us, we are to rejoice.'
